opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about quite often, because the two moments are so different.

When we started Microsoft Research China in 1998, the landscape was almost empty. China had very few world-class computing research labs, and the gap with the U.S. was enormous. The choice of directions was driven by a few principles. First, pick areas where we could reach the global frontier and publish at top venues like SIGGRAPH, CVPR, and ACL, because credibility was everything for a new lab. Second, pick areas that mattered to Microsoft's products: multimedia, speech, natural language, computer vision, the next-generation user interface. Third, pick areas where we could attract and nurture young talent. Many of the people who joined us then went on to found companies or lead research elsewhere. So the strategy was "basic research with long-term impact," and we were patient. We had a five- or ten-year horizon.

Today, at the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua, the context has changed completely. AI is no longer a niche academic field. It's the core technology driving the whole industry, and the pace is extraordinary. With large models, what used to take a decade now happens in a year or even a few months. And the big companies have far more compute, data, and engineering resources than any university institute. So we can't compete head-on with OpenAI, Google, or the leading Chinese model companies in training the biggest foundation model. That would be the wrong choice.

So how do we choose? I usually describe it in three ways.

First, we focus on problems that are important but that industry is not fully addressing, or not yet. For us that has meant three main areas: robotics and autonomous driving, which I call physical AI or embodied intelligence; AI for life sciences, things like biomedicine, drug discovery, and digital twins of the body; and green computing and AI for sustainability. These are fields where the large model is a tool, but the real breakthroughs require deep domain knowledge, real-world data, and long collaboration with industry.

Second, the word "industry" in our name is intentional. At MSR the question was whether we could do world-class research. Now the question is whether research can be translated into real industrial impact. We work closely with companies, sometimes incubating, sometimes co-developing, and we pick problems from real scenarios. Autonomous driving, for example, we did a lot of work with vehicle-road-cloud collaboration and open datasets, because that's something a single company can't do alone.

Third, the time horizon is different. At MSR we could take ten years. Today, if you think in ten-year cycles, the world will have changed three times before you finish. So we look for directions that are maybe three to five years ahead of industry, not twenty. Far enough to be research, close enough to matter.

One thing hasn't changed, though: talent. Then and now, the most important decision is not the topic, it's the people. If you have truly excellent young researchers with curiosity and the courage to work on hard problems, they'll find the right direction, often better than any plan you write down. That was true in 1998, and I think it's even more true in the age of AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes the earlier scarcity of world-class labs and emphasizes talent in both eras, but it does not say that research directions shifted from being constrained by the availability of field leaders to assuming leaders would be available.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the two situations are almost mirror images of each other.

When we started Microsoft Research in Beijing in 1998 and 1999, the hard problem was not choosing directions. The hard problem was convincing people that doing basic research in China was possible at all. We had almost no senior researchers, very few PhD students who had been trained to do open-ended work, and most of the industry around us was doing localization and outsourcing. So the strategy was fairly simple. We picked a few areas where we believed China could produce world-class talent, things like speech, multimedia, computer vision, graphics, user interfaces, and we let strong people go deep. The directions were set by the people we could hire, and by what Microsoft as a company needed five or ten years out. There was a lot of patience. Nobody expected a product in eighteen months.

Today the problem is reversed. Talent is abundant. China has an enormous number of very capable young researchers, and the infrastructure, the compute, the data, the open source ecosystem, all of that exists. The scarce thing now is judgment about where to place bets, because the field moves so fast that a direction can go from promising to crowded to obsolete within a year. When I built AIR at Tsinghua, I told the team that if a problem can be solved by a large company with enough GPUs and engineers, it is probably not the right problem for a university institute. We should not try to out-scale OpenAI or ByteDance. We should work on things where the time horizon is longer, where the problem is harder to define, or where an academic setting has a structural advantage, for example in fields that sit between disciplines.

So I pushed the institute toward three things. First, AI plus robotics and autonomous systems, where the physical world imposes constraints that pure language models do not face. Second, AI for science, especially biology, protein design, drug discovery, where domain knowledge matters as much as model capability. Third, the foundational questions, efficiency, safety, alignment, how do you get more intelligence out of less data and less compute. These are areas where a single breakthrough can change the direction of the whole field, and where you do not need to win on scale.

The other big difference is openness. At Microsoft Research we were part of one company, and in the end our work had to serve Windows and Office and later Bing. Today an institute has to decide its relationship with industry much more deliberately. I believe in a model where researchers can spin out companies, where students move freely between the lab and startups, and where the institute is a source of people and ideas rather than a competitor to the ecosystem. Several of our faculty have founded companies in autonomous driving and embodied AI, and I consider that a success, not a loss.

And honestly, the thing I worry about most now is the opposite of what I worried about in 1999. Back then I worried people would not take risks. Now I worry people take the same risk. Everyone chases the hot paper, the hot benchmark. A research institute's real value is in tolerating people who are working on something that looks irrelevant for a few years. That was true then, and I think it is even more true now.

r001.rationale: The response says early research directions were shaped by the people they could hire, when senior researchers were scarce. It contrasts that with abundant talent today, making the challenge choosing where to place bets.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that today we have to be much more selective. When we were building Microsoft Research in China, the task was to build a strong research organization: attract great people, create the right culture, and pursue important problems across a fairly broad range of computer science. There was a lot of room to establish new areas.

For an AI institute today, the landscape is much more crowded, and it changes very quickly. So the question is not simply, “Is this an important research direction?” It is also, “What can we contribute that others are unlikely to do?” If a project mainly requires more computing power, more data, and more engineers, a large company may be better positioned to pursue it. A research institute needs to find questions where a new idea or a longer-term commitment can make the difference.

I would look for a combination of fundamental scientific value, potential impact, and the strengths of the people we can bring together. You need a clear direction, but you also need to leave researchers enough freedom to surprise you. That balance has not changed: choose important problems, invest in excellent people, and be patient enough for something original to emerge.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from broad research building to greater selectivity in a crowded AI landscape, but it does not attribute that change to field leaders being unavailable before and expected to be available now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental principle is the same: you start with important problems and find the right people to work on them. But the environment today is very different.

When we were building Microsoft Research in China, a major task was to bring together talented researchers and give them the freedom to do world-class research. We had the support of a company, and there were many opportunities in areas such as speech, vision, and multimedia where a relatively small team could make a significant contribution.

Today, an AI institute has to be much more deliberate about where it can make a distinctive contribution. Some research directions require enormous amounts of computing, data, and engineering. You cannot simply follow every direction that the large companies are pursuing and expect to compete by doing the same thing with fewer resources.

So I would look at three things: Is the problem scientifically important? Do we have a particular strength in solving it? And, if we succeed, will it have a meaningful impact? That might lead you toward fundamental questions, or toward applying AI in a field where you have deep expertise and strong collaborators.

You also need a balance. Give people room to pursue ideas whose value may take years to become clear, while building enough shared focus that the institute becomes more than a collection of individual projects. The technology changes very quickly, but choosing good people and asking good questions remain the foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s institute must choose areas where it can contribute distinctively, considering resources, strengths, and impact. It does not describe a shift from limited availability of field leaders to leaders now being expected to be available.
